Medical Brain / GHS402 / Pharmacology

Ky's GHS402 Pharmacology Study Guide

Gastrointestinal and CNS pharmacology from the GHS402 lecture decks, one section per class. Every drug is taken from the slides.

1. Antiemetics and Prokinetic Agents

Lecture scope: Lecture 1: the emetic pathway and its four afferent inputs, and the antiemetic and prokinetic drug classes (anticholinergics, H1 antihistamines, prokinetics, 5-HT3 antagonists, neuroleptics, NK1 antagonist, cannabinoids): mechanism, use and adverse effects.

Slide decks: Pharm 1, Antiemetics and Prokinetic Agents (20 Qs)

Vomiting is a coordinated reflex with a pre-ejection phase, retching and ejection, driven by the vomiting center in the nucleus tractus solitarius. Four afferent inputs feed that center: the chemoreceptor trigger zone (outside the blood-brain barrier), the vestibular system, the GI tract and higher CNS centers. Each input carries its own receptors, so the right antiemetic is the one that blocks the receptor on the pathway causing the vomiting. Prokinetic agents speed gastric emptying and overlap with the antiemetics through dopamine blockade.

The 5-HT3 antagonists share one mechanism and differ by half-life and QT risk. The dopamine-blocking prokinetics differ in whether they enter the brain: metoclopramide crosses the blood-brain barrier, whereas domperidone does not cross the barrier but acts on the CTZ and causes no EPS. Vestibular and anticholinergic agents treat motion sickness and pregnancy nausea.

High-Yield Notes

Start from the cause of vomiting in the third column, then read back to the input and receptors and across to the drugs. Ondansetron appears at both the CTZ and the GI tract, while the higher CNS row names no receptors and lists benzodiazepines among its drugs.

InputReceptorsVomiting caused byDrugs
CTZ (area postrema)D2, 5-HT3, NK1Blood-borne emeticsOndansetron, metoclopramide, domperidone, aprepitant
Vestibular system (cranial nerve VIII)M1, H1Motion sicknessScopolamine; meclizine, diphenhydramine
GI tract (vagus)5-HT3Chemotherapy, radiotherapy, enteritisOndansetron, granisetron, dolasetron, palonosetron
Higher CNSNone namedAnxiety, anticipatory vomitingBenzodiazepines, dronabinol, prochlorperazine, promethazine, chlorpromazine, haloperidol

Read the half-life column against the adverse effects column. Ondansetron runs 3 to 5 hours with QT prolongation, palonosetron about 40 hours with less QT prolongation, and dolasetron carries a higher QT risk. The use column also carries a feature for most drugs, such as the granisetron transdermal patch.

Read the mechanism column first, then the adverse effects. Metoclopramide crosses the blood-brain barrier and carries tardive dyskinesia, while domperidone does not cross the barrier but acts on the CTZ, and has no EPS. Mosapride and itopride are listed with the same adverse effects, and cisapride and tegaserod are listed as prokinetics.

DrugMechanismUseAdverse effects
MetoclopramideD2 block in CTZ and gut, 5-HT4 agonism raising ACh release, 5-HT3 block at higher dose; crosses the blood-brain barrierGastroparesis, GERD, chemotherapy and postoperative vomiting; not preferred in motion sickness; gastrokinetic before emergency general anesthesia and for duodenal intubationSedation, diarrhoea, dystonias, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia, galactorrhoea, gynaecomastia; enters milk: suckling infant loose motions, dystonias
DomperidonePeripheral D2 antagonist; does not cross the barrier but acts on the CTZPreferred antiemetic in children and parkinsonism; vomiting from drug overdosage, uremia, neurological injury; GERDDry mouth, loose stools, headache, hyperprolactinemia, galactorrhoea; no EPS
Mosapride5-HT4 agonist, ACh release from myenteric neuronsProkinetic only, motility disorders and GERDAbdominal pain, loose stool, headache

Cisapride, tegaserodNot statedListed as prokinetics; cisapride withdrawn from the marketNot stated

Hyoscine (scopolamine) is an antimuscarinic (M1) that blocks afferents to the vomiting center. It has a brief action and a transdermal patch, is used for motion sickness, and causes dry mouth and sedation. Dicyclomine is an anticholinergic used for motion sickness and morning sickness prophylaxis, as the deck states; its adverse effects are not stated. Meclizine is an H1 antihistamine with long duration, used for sea sickness, and causes sedation.

Promethazine and diphenhydramine are H1 antihistamines with antimuscarinic action and 4 to 6 hours protection. With metoclopramide the effect is additive and counters EPS. They are used for motion sickness and morning sickness, and cause sedation and anticholinergic effects. Doxylamine is a sedative H1 antihistamine with pyridoxine, about 10 hours, used for morning sickness, at bedtime; it causes drowsiness, dry mouth and vertigo. Cinnarizine is an antivertigo drug that inhibits Ca influx in endolymph, used for vertigo; its adverse effects are not stated. For cyclizine, the mechanism, use and adverse effects are not stated.

The remaining classes cover refractory or central causes of vomiting. Chlorpromazine, prochlorperazine, haloperidol, droperidol and trifluoperazine are each D2 block in the CTZ, so read the use and adverse effects columns to tell them apart: chlorpromazine is more sedating, trifluoperazine less sedating, and haloperidol and droperidol both carry QT prolongation. Aprepitant (NK1) and dronabinol, nabilone (CB1) differ in mechanism.

DrugMechanismUseAdverse effects
AprepitantNK1 antagonist; blocks Substance P in NTS and CTZAcute and delayed CINV, with a 5-HT3 antagonist and dexamethasoneFatigue
ChlorpromazineD2 block in the CTZRefractory vomiting, hiccups; more sedatingSedation, hypotension, anticholinergic
ProchlorperazineD2 block in the CTZVomiting, labyrinthine vertigo, migraineSedation, EPS, hypotension
HaloperidolD2 block in the CTZRefractory vomiting, palliative care, migraine-associated vomitingEPS, akathisia, QT prolongation
DroperidolD2 block in the CTZPONV, refractory vomitingSedation, hypotension, QT prolongation
TrifluoperazineD2 block in the CTZVomiting, intractable hiccups; less sedatingEPS, sedation, hypotension
Dronabinol, nabiloneCB1 agonistsRefractory CINV, appetite in cachexiaEuphoria, hallucinations, tachycardia, dry mouth, red conjunctiva
Points that carry questions
  • Retching is rhythmic respiratory muscle action against a closed glottis before ejection.
  • Dexamethasone and benzodiazepines are named as other antiemetics with no mechanism taught.
  • Metoclopramide blocks 5-HT3 only at high dose, which also raises EPS, so a 5-HT3 antagonist is preferred for chemotherapy vomiting.
  • Cannabinoids are contraindicated in pregnancy and severe psychiatric illness.

2. Acid Peptic Disease Drugs

Lecture scope: Lecture 2: causes of gastric acid hypersecretion and H. pylori testing, parietal cell acid secretion and its regulation, and the drugs for acid peptic disease (antacids, PPIs, H2 antagonists, misoprostol, pirenzepine, sucralfate, bismuth) with H. pylori regimens, uses, adverse effects and interactions.

Slide decks: Pharm 2, Drugs Used in Acid Peptic Diseases (18 Qs)

A peptic ulcer is a mucosal break reaching the submucosa, and it forms when hostile factors (H. pylori, gastric acid, pepsin, NSAIDs) outweigh protective ones (bicarbonate, prostaglandins, mucus, mucosal blood flow). Parietal cells make the acid: histamine, acetylcholine and gastrin drive the H+K+ATPase proton pump, while somatostatin and PGE2 hold it back. Each drug class works at one point on that pathway, so the drug to choose is the one that matches the step it blocks, neutralizes or protects. The deck's modern view is that eradicating H. pylori and treating NSAID ulcer is the mainstay, with acid suppression still important.

PPIs and H2 blockers are the two most used classes, and they are compared here by target and acid cut. PPIs (omeprazole) block the H+K+ATPase irreversibly at the final step and cut 80 to 85% of daily acid, whereas H2 blockers compete reversibly with histamine at the H2 receptor and cut over 90% of nocturnal acid and 60 to 70% of daytime acid. PPIs are more effective in GERD and are the drug of choice in Zollinger-Ellison. Misoprostol, a PGE1 analogue, is the most specific for NSAID ulcer and is contraindicated in pregnancy, and cimetidine brings gynaecomastia and is a strong CYP inhibitor.

High-Yield Notes

Read each row across from the drug to the step it acts on, then to its signature adverse effect in the last column. Omeprazole is the PPI prototype and cimetidine the H2 prototype, while misoprostol is a PGE1 analogue and pirenzepine a selective M1 blocker. Check the Use column for which drug suits GERD, Zollinger-Ellison or NSAID ulcer.

DrugMechanismUseAdverse effects, interactions
Omeprazole (PPI prototype)Prodrug turned into sulfenamide; irreversible H+K+ATPase block; 80 to 85% less acid; lasts 24 to 48 h, half-life 0.5 to 2 hGERD, ulcer, NSAID ulcer, Zollinger-Ellison; beats H2 blockersB12 deficiency, hip fracture; inhibits CYP2C19 and 3A4 (warfarin, diazepam, phenytoin)
Cimetidine (H2 prototype)Reversible competition with histamine at basolateral H2 receptor; least potentDuodenal and gastric ulcer, stress ulcer; not first choice in GERD or Zollinger-EllisonGynaecomastia, galactorrhoea, impotence, confusion; strong CYP inhibitor
Ranitidine, famotidineSame; ranitidine 5 times, famotidine 30 times cimetidineBlock over 90% of nocturnal acidHeadache, constipation; ranitidine has no anti-androgen effect
MisoprostolPGE1 analogue: less acid, more mucus and bicarbonateMost specific for NSAID ulcerDiarrhea, colic; contraindicated in pregnancy
PirenzepineSelective M1 blockerDuodenal ulcerFew anticholinergic effects

PPIs and H2 blockers are the two most used classes; compare them directly.

PPIs (omeprazole) hit the H+K+ATPase, irreversibly, at the final step, and cut 80 to 85% of daily acid. They are more effective in GERD and the drug of choice in Zollinger-Ellison, at a higher dose. They heal duodenal, gastric and NSAID ulcer and go into H. pylori regimens. Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, 3A4, and low acid alters ketoconazole, digoxin. Give them on an empty stomach, enteric coated; pantoprazole can be given IV.

H2 blockers (cimetidine, famotidine) compete reversibly with histamine at the H2 receptor. They cut over 90% nocturnal acid and 60 to 70% of daytime acid, and are less effective in GERD and in Zollinger-Ellison. For ulcer healing, duodenal is 60 to 85% at 4 weeks and 70 to 95% at 8, gastric is 50 to 75% at 8, and stress ulcer is also treated. Cimetidine inhibits CYP1A2, 2C9, 2D6, 3A4 (warfarin, theophylline, phenytoin), and antacids cut absorption, with a 2 hour gap. Dosing is not stated.

Antacids neutralize acid and protectives coat the ulcer. For the three antacids, the Action column gives site and speed: sodium bicarbonate is systemic and rapid, while aluminium hydroxide is non-systemic and slow and magnesium hydroxide is non-systemic and fast. Then read Key points for the adverse effect or restriction that goes with each agent, from constipation to black stools.

AgentActionKey points
Sodium bicarbonateSystemic, rapidCO2, sodium load, alkalosis, rebound
Aluminium hydroxideNon-systemic, slowConstipation
Magnesium hydroxideNon-systemic, fastDiarrhea; combine with aluminium
SucralfateGel at pH below 4Not with antacids; not for NSAID ulcer; constipation, hypophosphataemia
Bismuth subcitrateCoat; PGE2, mucus; kills H. pyloriBlack stools

Eradication needs combinations for healing and eradication, about 90% successful. Read down the Regimen column against Duration: triple and quadruple run 14 days and sequential runs 10 days. Then read Components for what changes, noting that sequential splits days 1 to 5 from days 6 to 10.

RegimenDurationComponents
Triple14 daysPPI, clarithromycin, amoxicillin or metronidazole
Quadruple14 daysPPI, bismuth, tetracycline, metronidazole
Sequential10 daysDays 1 to 5 PPI, amoxicillin; days 6 to 10 PPI, clarithromycin, tinidazole
Points that carry questions
  • Duodenal ulcer is five times commoner, hunger pain relieved by eating; gastric pain follows eating with weight loss.
  • Non-invasive H. pylori tests: breath, serology, stool antigen; invasive: urease, histology, culture.
  • NSAIDs raise ulcer risk four times, aspirin two times; SSRIs, corticosteroids or anticoagulants add bleeding risk; stop the NSAID and give a PPI 6 to 8 weeks, and if it must continue, COX-2 NSAID plus PPI protects best.
  • Sucralfate blocks absorption of tetracyclines, FQs, H2 blockers, phenytoin; antacids cut bismuth efficacy.
  • H. pylori spreads oral-oral and fecal-oral; somatostatin (antral D cells) and PGE2 inhibit acid.
  • Named without mechanism: magnesium trisilicate, magaldrate, carbenoxolone; enprostil and rioprostil are PGE2 analogues.
  • Metronidazole blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase: alcohol on quadruple therapy gives flushing and vomiting.

3. Laxatives and Antidiarrheals

Lecture scope: Lecture 3: the classes of drugs used for diarrhea and constipation, their mechanisms and therapeutic roles: rehydration, zinc, antimicrobials and probiotics, antisecretory and antimotility antidiarrheals, bulk, osmotic, surfactant, lubricant and stimulant laxatives and purgatives, and the drugs for inflammatory bowel disease (5-ASA compounds, corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, TNF alpha inhibitors), with their uses, adverse effects and patient-specific cautions.

Slide decks: Pharm 3, Laxatives and Antidiarrheals (29 Qs)

Diarrhea (3 or more loose or watery stools in 24 hours) kills mainly through dehydration, so management starts with rehydration and nutrition, and drugs come last.

Constipation is a symptom, not a disease: fewer than three motions a week, with straining and a sense of incomplete evacuation. Each drug works by changing one thing: how much water the gut secretes or holds, how fast it moves, or how inflamed it is. The drug to choose is the one that matches that step, and the safety question is usually the infection, the age or the organ that the drug would harm.

High-Yield Notes

Sort the antidiarrheals by what they do to secretion and motility. Read the Mechanism column: ORS replaces water, racecadotril gives less secretion, hyoscyamine and dicyclomine slow motility, and loperamide and diphenoxylate are opioids. The contrast is no BBB entry for loperamide against crosses BBB for diphenoxylate.

ZincGiven with low osmolarity ORS in children under 5Shortens illness; 20 mg a day (6 to 60 months), 10 mg (0 to 6 months) for 10 to 14 days cuts recurrence

Antimicrobials help only in severe disease; antimotility drugs are contraindicated in invasive infection.

Most traveller's diarrhea is ETEC, and cotrimoxazole, norfloxacin and doxycycline are named. For EPEC, antimotility drugs are contraindicated; cotrimoxazole or a fluoroquinolone is named. Shigella is treated only when there is blood or mucus, with no antimotility drug; ciprofloxacin or norfloxacin is named. For nontyphoid Salmonella enteritis a fluoroquinolone, cotrimoxazole or ampicillin is named. For Yersinia enterocolitica in severe cases cotrimoxazole is named, with ciprofloxacin as an alternative. Probiotics (Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, Streptococcus faecalis, Enterococcus, yeast Saccharomyces boulardii) cut antibiotic-associated and traveller's diarrhea.

Laxatives give soft formed stool, purgatives give watery evacuation and complete cleansing. Read the Mechanism column for bulk, surfactant, lubricant, saline, osmotic and irritant agents, then the last column for any adverse effect.

IBD drugs: 5-ASA acts locally in the colon; steroids treat flares, others maintain remission. Read the Role column to place each drug, from the 5-ASA drugs to prednisolone, azathioprine, methotrexate, cyclosporine and the anti-TNF drugs, then the last column for any adverse effect.

Points that carry questions
  • Acute diarrhea lasts under 2 weeks (90% infectious); persistent 2 to 4 weeks; chronic over 4 weeks.
  • IV rehydration if loss exceeds 10% body weight or 10 ml/kg/hr, or the patient cannot drink.
  • Home ORS: 8 teaspoons sugar and 1 teaspoon salt in 1 litre of boiled, cooled water.
  • Loperamide complication in young children: toxic megacolon.
  • Laxative abuse: an emptied colon refills slowly, so the patient needs daily laxatives.
  • Bristol chart: type 1 severe constipation, type 7 severe diarrhea.
  • Crohn: granulomatous, mouth to anus; UC: non-granulomatous, rectum upward; a 5-ASA enema suits rectal or distal UC.
  • Octreotide dose 100 microgram subcutaneously twice or three times daily.
  • Oral 5-ASA is over 80% absorbed in the proximal intestine, so an inert carrier (sulfapyridine, azo bond, aminobenzoyl-beta-alanine) cuts absorption and delivers it to the colon.
  • Methotrexate gives stomatitis because it lowers the folic acid pathway (Class notes, IBD drugs, 6 Oct 2026).
  • Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase: azathioprine toxicity, pancytopenia.
  • Opioids contract biliary smooth muscle and the sphincter of Oddi: right upper quadrant colic.

4. Introduction to Neuropharmacology

Lecture scope: Lecture 4: what neuropharmacology covers, the five steps of neurotransmission, ionotropic against metabotropic receptors, how each major CNS transmitter system (glutamate, GABA, acetylcholine, dopamine, serotonin, norepinephrine, opioid peptides) is modulated by drugs at synthesis, release, reuptake, metabolism or receptor, and how transmitter abnormalities relate to disease.

Slide decks: Pharm 4, Introduction to Neuropharmacology (23 Qs)

Neuropharmacology asks how drugs change neurotransmission, and every drug in this overview works at one step of the same chain: action potential (sodium channel block), calcium entry, vesicle fusion (SNARE proteins), receptor binding (EPSP or IPSP) and termination by reuptake or enzymatic breakdown. For each transmitter the deck draws the same synapse, and a drug is placed by the step it blocks: synthesis, storage, release, receptor, or reuptake and metabolism.

The receptor family then tells you how fast the effect is and what second messenger follows. Ionotropic receptors are ligand-gated channels that act in milliseconds, while Gs stimulates, Gi inhibits, Gq gives Ca2+ and contraction. D1 is a Gs receptor and D2 a Gi receptor, and antipsychotics block D2.

High-Yield Notes

Receptor family decides speed and signalling; Gs stimulates, Gi inhibits, Gq gives Ca2+ and contraction. Read the Signal column for what each family does and the last column for the receptors the deck names in it. The contrast is between Gs, where adenylyl cyclase and cAMP go up, and Gi, where they go down, while Gq works through IP3 and DAG.

FamilySignalReceptors named
IonotropicLigand-gated channel, millisecondsAMPA, NMDA, kainate; GABA-A, glycine (Cl-); nicotinic ACh; 5-HT3
GsAdenylyl cyclase up, cAMP up, PKABeta-1, beta-2, D1, 5-HT4/6/7
GiAdenylyl cyclase down, cAMP down, K+ channels openAlpha-2, D2, M2/M4, opioid, GABA-B, 5-HT1
GqPhospholipase C: IP3 (Ca2+) and DAG (PKC)Alpha-1, M1/M3/M5, 5-HT2, H1

Each transmitter slide marks the step and the drug, so match step to drug. Read across a row from the transmitter to the step and the drug named at it, then to the receptor and its signal. Most rows list a transporter drug beside an enzyme drug, for example dopamine and serotonin, while the opioid peptides row has no reuptake pump and only peptidases.

One D2 blocker acts in all four dopamine pathways, which explains antipsychotic adverse effects. Read the Function column beside the last column for each pathway: the mesolimbic and mesocortical rows give the effect on positive and negative symptoms, while the nigrostriatal and tuberoinfundibular rows give parkinsonism and hyperprolactinemia.

PathwayFunctionEffect of D2 block
MesolimbicReward; psychosis if raisedFewer positive symptoms
MesocorticalCognition, motivationWorse negative symptoms
NigrostriatalMotor controlParkinsonism (EPS)
TuberoinfundibularInhibits prolactinHyperprolactinemia

Interactions and overdose each have a named antidote or fix. Read the Features column to recognise the problem and the last column for the management. Miosis sits with opioid overdose and mydriasis with anticholinergic toxicity, while clonus is listed for serotonin syndrome and raised CK for neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

ProblemFeaturesManagement
Opioid overdoseMiosis, coma, respiratory depressionNaloxone, repeated
Anticholinergic toxicityDry, hot, flushed, mydriasis, deliriumPhysostigmine, supportive
Benzodiazepine overdoseSedation, respiratory depression with co-ingestantsAirway; flumazenil only with caution

Several drugs carry a signature point the slides state outright, most of them a signature toxicity. Clozapine causes agranulocytosis and seizures, and aripiprazole is an atypical antipsychotic that is a partial agonist. TCAs give QRS widening in overdose. Triptans give vasoconstriction: avoid in coronary disease. Bupropion causes seizures, and clonidine gives rebound hypertension on withdrawal. Buprenorphine has a ceiling on respiratory depression, and tramadol brings seizures and serotonin syndrome. Benzodiazepine or alcohol withdrawal brings seizures and delirium tremens.

Points that carry questions
  • Benzodiazepines raise Cl- channel opening frequency (need GABA); barbiturates raise duration.
  • BBB crossing: small, lipophilic, un-ionized, low protein binding; levodopa uses LAT1, carbidopa cannot cross; P-gp excludes loperamide.
  • CYP inducers: carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampin, St John's wort; CYP inhibitors: fluvoxamine, fluoxetine, grapefruit, ketoconazole.
  • Long-term levodopa brings on-off fluctuations and dyskinesia, from its short half-life; adding entacapone (COMT) smooths the on-off effect (Class notes, neuropharmacology, 6 Oct 2026).
  • Lipophilic thiopental wakes fast by redistribution despite a long half-life.
  • Tolerance needs a bigger dose (opioids, benzodiazepines); sensitization is reverse tolerance (stimulants).
  • Chronic antagonist gives upregulation, chronic agonist downregulation: tardive dyskinesia is D2 upregulation.
  • SSRI effect is delayed 2 to 6 weeks; narrow index: lithium, phenytoin, TCAs.
  • The mood stabilizer lithium works by inositol/GSK-3 modulation, with a narrow index: tremor and nephrotoxicity (Class notes, lithium, 12 Oct 2026).

5. Antipsychotics

Lecture scope: Lecture 5: schizophrenia and its neurochemical basis (dopamine and serotonin hypotheses), how classical and atypical antipsychotics compare on positive and negative symptoms, their uses beyond schizophrenia, their adverse-effect profiles, and the time course, signs and treatment of extrapyramidal symptoms.

Slide decks: Pharm 5, Antipsychotics (20 Qs)

Antipsychotics treat psychosis, a distorted sense of reality, chiefly in schizophrenia. The old dopamine hypothesis says excess dopamine drives positive symptoms, so D2 blockade works; the serotonin hypothesis adds 5-HT2A blockade for the newer drugs. Dopamine runs in four pathways, so one D2 blocker gives the benefit and the harm together: relief in the mesolimbic path, movement disorders in the nigrostriatal path, and prolactin rise in the tuberoinfundibular path. What separates the drugs is how hard they block D2 and which other receptors they hit.

Among the typical drugs, high potency haloperidol, fluphenazine and trifluoperazine give more EPS with less sedation and less anticholinergic effect, while low potency chlorpromazine and thioridazine give more sedation and anticholinergic effects with less EPS. The atypical drugs block 5-HT2A and D2, treat negative as well as positive symptoms, and carry lower EPS and prolactin risk. Each atypical has a signature: clozapine agranulocytosis, olanzapine high metabolic syndrome risk, quetiapine sedation, risperidone high prolactin, ziprasidone QT prolongation, and aripiprazole D2 partial agonism.

High-Yield Notes

Typical drugs block D2 only; atypical drugs block 5-HT2A and D2. For the typical (first generation) drugs the clinical dose tracks D2 affinity. The drugs are the phenothiazines: chlorpromazine, fluphenazine, trifluoperazine, thioridazine (slide 10 prints it under thioxanthenes); and the butyrophenone haloperidol. They reduce positive symptoms (mesolimbic D2), with more EPS and hyperprolactinemia. Some atypical (second generation) drugs also block D4, alpha 1, H1. The drugs are the heterocyclic structures: clozapine, olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, ziprasidone, aripiprazole. They treat positive plus negative symptoms (5-HT2A block raises mesocortical dopamine), with lower EPS and prolactin risk.

Typicals split by potency: the stronger the D2 block, the more EPS. High potency haloperidol, fluphenazine and trifluoperazine give more EPS, less sedation and less anticholinergic effect. Low potency chlorpromazine and thioridazine give more sedation and anticholinergic effects, and less EPS.

Each atypical has a signature to recognise. Clozapine brings agranulocytosis; most effective for treatment-resistant schizophrenia; strong alpha 1, H1, M1 block; metabolic risk; similar D1 and D2 affinity (slide 6); D4 << 5HT (slide 8). Olanzapine carries high metabolic syndrome risk (weight gain, diabetes), and is used in acute mania; D2 << 5HT2A (slide 8). Quetiapine causes sedation, and is used in bipolar depression (slide 13) and acute mania (slide 20). Risperidone gives high prolactin (galactorrhea, amenorrhea) and dose-dependent EPS. Paliperidone is the active metabolite of risperidone, with a similar profile. Ziprasidone brings QT prolongation and the least weight gain; D2 << 5HT2A and 5HT1D (slide 8). Aripiprazole is a D2 partial agonist (partial dopamine agonist, slide 8), with minimal metabolic effects; switch for EPS.

EPS lengthen with duration of treatment and are mostly due to typical drugs. Read the Timing column for the onset of each syndrome, from hours to days for acute dystonia to months to years for tardive dyskinesia. Then read across to the Features and Treatment columns to match each syndrome to its treatment, and note that the neuroleptic malignant syndrome row carries a rare-condition note in place of a timing.

SyndromeTimingFeaturesTreatment
Acute dystoniaHours to daysSpasm of tongue, face, neck, upward eye movementBenztropine or diphenhydramine, IM or IV
AkathisiaDays to weeksMotor restlessness, cannot remain seatedPropranolol, benzodiazepine, muscarinic blocker
ParkinsonismWeeks to monthsBradykinesia, rest tremor, rigidity, shuffling gaitLower dose; benztropine or amantadine
Tardive dyskinesiaMonths to yearsOrofacial dyskinesia, tongue protrusion, athetosisValbenazine (slide 14) is the treatment; slide 17 says no effective drug
Neuroleptic malignant syndromeRare condition (slide 19)Fever, rigidity, altered mental status and stupor, impairment of sweating (slide 19 wording), unstable BP, myoglobinemiaWithdraw drug; dantrolene, bromocriptine, diazepam

Antipsychotics are used beyond schizophrenia. In schizophrenia the use is primary and long term, with antidepressants, lithium or valproic acid. In bipolar disorder, acute mania takes olanzapine or quetiapine (slide 20), and quetiapine also treats bipolar depression (slide 13). Gilles de la Tourette's syndrome (motor and vocal tics, childhood onset) is a further use. In Alzheimer's or Parkinson's psychosis, and stimulant psychosis, the antipsychotic treats the psychosis. For nausea and vomiting, low-dose chlorpromazine or haloperidol is used, by D2 block at the CTZ.

Points that carry questions
  • Dopamine hypothesis (slide 6): dopamine agonists (amphetamine or levodopa) induce psychosis; typical antipsychotics strongly block D2; dopamine receptor density is increased in untreated patients.
  • Glutamate (slide 8): PCP, an NMDA antagonist, produces schizophrenia-like symptoms.
  • Serotonin hypothesis (slide 9): LSD and mescaline (serotonin agonists) cause hallucinations.
  • Symptoms: positive (delusions, hallucinations); negative (apathy, avolition, alogia); cognitive (poor working memory).
  • EPS mechanism: blocked D2 on the cholinergic interneuron gives enhanced ACh release at M1, so antimuscarinics reverse it.
  • Mesocortical dopamine hypoactivity gives negative and cognitive symptoms; mesolimbic excess gives positive ones.
  • Akathisia is the most common EPS, while acute dystonia is the first to appear (Class notes, antipsychotics, 7 Oct 2026).
  • Receptor to side effect: strong M1 block gives dry mouth, strong H1 block gives sedation and weight gain, strong alpha 1 block gives postural hypotension (Class notes, antipsychotics, 7 Oct 2026).
  • Asenapine appears only on a slide 9 diagram of 5-HT2C inverse agonists, with no teaching attached.

6. Antidepressants

Lecture scope: Lecture 6: the neurochemical and neurotrophic theories of affect and how antidepressants modulate them, the major antidepressant classes (SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics, MAO inhibitors, serotonin modulators and the atypical agents) with their cellular targets, their use in non-depressive disorders, a comparison of adverse effects and mechanisms across classes, and recognition and management of serotonin syndrome.

Slide decks: Pharm 6, Antidepressant Drugs (37 Qs) · Pharm 4, Introduction to Neuropharmacology (12 Qs) · Pharm 6 review, Antidepressants Review (26 Qs) · Pharm 6, Antidepressants (class deck) (15 Qs)

Depression (major depressive disorder) is low mood most of the time for at least 2 weeks and/or loss of interest or pleasure, with disturbed sleep and appetite, poor energy and cognition, and thoughts of guilt and suicide. The monoamine hypothesis blames too little serotonin, norepinephrine or dopamine, but it cannot be the whole account, because drugs raise synaptic amines promptly while relief takes 3 to 4 weeks. The neurotrophic hypothesis adds that raised cortisol lowers BDNF, so the hippocampus shrinks. Beyond major depression the deck names persistent depressive disorder (low grade, beginning two years before diagnosis), seasonal affective disorder (winter), psychotic depression, postpartum depression, premenstrual dysphoric disorder and atypical depression, in which a positive event briefly lifts mood and appetite and sleep rise (PH6C, slides 10 to 19).

The classes below differ in which carrier or receptor they hit, and so in what they cost the patient. SSRIs block SERT only, while SNRIs and TCAs block SERT and NET. TCAs also block alpha-1, H1 and muscarinic receptors, which is why they bring orthostatic hypotension, sedation and dry mouth, whereas SNRIs have no antihistamine, alpha-blocking or antimuscarinic effect and instead raise BP and HR. Bupropion is a weak NE and DA reuptake inhibitor with no 5-HT effect and lowers the seizure threshold, mirtazapine blocks the presynaptic alpha-2 receptor, and the MAOIs block MAO. MAO-A metabolises norepinephrine and serotonin and is inhibited by moclobemide, whereas MAO-B metabolises dopamine and is inhibited by selegiline; milnacipran is an SNRI and mianserin an atypical agent (PH6C, slides 25, 30 and 36). Bupropion is also a non-competitive nicotinic antagonist (PH6C, slide 33). Bipolar depression is treated as depression, but mania needs a mood stabilizer. Lithium, a small monovalent cation, is the gold standard (about 80% effective in acute mania, 60% long term) but is being replaced because its therapeutic ratio is narrow (PH6C, slide 44; Class notes, Antidepressants, 9 Oct 2026). It inhibits the enzymes that recycle membrane inositol phosphates, so less PIP2 is regenerated and less IP3 and DAG is released (slide 45). Its half-life is about 20 hours (36 in the elderly) and it is cleared almost entirely by the kidney, so the target is 0.8 to 1.2 mEq/L, drawn 10 to 12 hours after the last dose (slide 46). Diuretics, NSAIDs, metronidazole and ACE inhibitors reduce clearance and cause toxicity, while acetazolamide, urea, xanthines (caffeine) and alkalinizing agents raise clearance and lower the level (slide 47). Lithium causes tremor (reduced by propranolol or atenolol), sedation, ataxia, edema, and a reversible nephrogenic diabetes insipidus that is resistant to vasopressin and treated with amiloride (slide 48; Class notes, Antidepressants, 9 Oct 2026). Atypical antipsychotics (olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone) are also used, and olanzapine with fluoxetine is the deck's example for the depressive phase (slides 34 and 44).

Serotonin signalling ends mainly by reuptake through SERT (about 80 to 90%), with MAO-A removing about 10 to 20%, so SSRIs and MAOIs both raise synaptic serotonin. The receptors are told apart by coupling. 5-HT1A is the Gi somatodendritic autoreceptor of the raphe nuclei and lowers 5-HT release, and 5-HT1B/1D (triptans) is also Gi, giving cranial vasoconstriction. 5-HT2A, 2B and 2C are Gq: 2B drives valve fibroblast proliferation (fenfluramine, pergolide and cabergoline cause valvulopathy), and trazodone's 5-HT2A block lowers sexual side effects. 5-HT4 is Gs (GI motility), and 5-HT3 alone is a ligand-gated channel, the target of ondansetron and granisetron. SSRIs can cause SIADH with dilutional hyponatremia (confusion, seizures), and stopping abruptly gives a discontinuation syndrome (anxiety, irritability, confusion, crying), so titrate down over 2 weeks or longer; paroxetine carries first-trimester heart defects. In TCA overdose, bicarbonate raises serum sodium and pH and so reduces sodium channel block (QRS over 100 ms, hypotension, ventricular arrhythmia). Antidepressants can precipitate mania in underlying bipolar disorder, as with venlafaxine.

High-Yield Notes

Read each row from the middle column to the last: the target blocked explains the adverse effects. The TCA row is longest because TCAs also block alpha-1, H1, muscarinic receptors and ion channels. Trazodone and nefazodone are the potent 5-HT2 blockers, and the MAOI row carries the tyramine reaction and a timing rule.

ClassDrugs, targetSignature adverse effects
SSRIsFluoxetine, paroxetine, citalopram, escitalopram, fluvoxamine, sertraline; block SERT onlySexual dysfunction and drowsiness (17% each), weight gain, insomnia, anxiety, nausea; QT prolongation, most with citalopram
SNRIsVenlafaxine, desvenlafaxine, duloxetine, milnacipran (levomilnacipran); block SERT and NET; no antihistamine, alpha-blocking or antimuscarinic effectDiarrhea, vomiting; raised BP and HR, insomnia, anxiety, agitation; sweating and urinary retention; duloxetine liver toxicity
TCAsAmitriptyline, imipramine, desipramine and others; block SERT and NET; clomipramine favours SERTAlpha-1 block: orthostatic hypotension; H1 block: weight gain, sedation; antimuscarinic: dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary hesitancy; K channel block (PH6, slide 28): QT, torsades; standard overdose mechanism Na channel block, QRS widening (PH4, slide 17; PH6B, slides 26 and 28); seizures

SSRIs are mostly CYP P450 substrates and inhibitors, so an interaction follows whichever isozyme the drug inhibits. Fluoxetine and paroxetine inhibit 2D6 potently, fluvoxamine inhibits 1A2 and 2C19 potently, and citalopram and escitalopram inhibit none; the last column holds a distinguishing point where one is taught.

SSRIMain CYP isozymes inhibitedOther points
Fluoxetine2D6 (potent), 2C9, 2C19, 2B6, 3A4Metabolite norfluoxetine, half-life 4 to 16 days (others 20 to 30 h)
Fluvoxamine1A2 (potent), 2C19 (potent), 2B6, 2C9, 3A4Named for OCD
Paroxetine2D6 (potent), 2B6 (potent)
Sertraline2D6 (potent at high doses), 2B6, 2C9, 2C19, 3A4

Serotonin syndrome follows several serotonergic drugs: an SSRI blocks SERT and an MAOI blocks MAO-A, so serotonin overstimulates 5-HT1A and 5-HT2A within hours of starting, raising or adding a drug, with mental status, autonomic and neuromuscular (hyperreflexia, clonus) signs. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is the look-alike: rigidity, fever, raised CK and autonomic instability after an antipsychotic, without clonus, treated by stopping it and giving dantrolene or bromocriptine. The table gives features and management by stage.

StageFeaturesManagement
MildMydriasis, shivering, sweating, mild tachycardiaObserve at least 6 h; benzodiazepines
ModerateAgitation, disorientation; rigidity, tachycardia, temperature above 40 C; tremor, clonus, hyperreflexiaAdmit, cardiac monitoring, cyproheptadine
Life threateningDelirium, hypertension, hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, tachycardiaICU, esmolol or nitroprusside, cooling, sedation, paralysis, ventilation

Because MAO-A also metabolises dietary tyramine, an MAOI with tyramine (aged cheese, cured meats, soy products, beer, wine) or pseudoephedrine releases norepinephrine and causes hypertensive crisis, treated with phentolamine. The selegiline patch carries a much lower risk. Bupropion causes tachycardia but no sexual effects, weight gain or sedation, and is a problem in epilepsy, alcoholism and eating disorders. Mirtazapine is useful in depression with insomnia, anorexia or weight loss. Trazodone priapism is rare (1 in 1,000 to 10,000).

Valproic acid, lamotrigine and carbamazepine are antiseizure drugs used for mania. Read from the drug to its place in bipolar disorder, then to the adverse effect or test that tells it apart.

DrugPlace in bipolar disorderAdverse effect or monitoring
Valproic acidFirst choice in acute mania in the US; works in lithium non-responders; Na+ and T-type Ca2+ channels, more GABAHepatic damage, teratogenicity (neural tube defects per class notes); monitor liver function, platelets, ammonia; inhibits CYP
LamotrigineMaintenance; bipolar depression; Na+ and Ca2+ channel blockSlow titration for Stevens-Johnson syndrome, slower with valproate
CarbamazepineMania and maintenance (not FDA-approved); Na+ channel blockAgranulocytosis, leukopenia; late hyponatremia in elderly cardiac patients

Uses beyond depression are named by drug. For major depression, SSRIs, SNRIs, 5-HT antagonists are preferred over TCAs for tolerability. Panic disorder takes SSRIs or venlafaxine, and OCD takes clomipramine or an SSRI (especially fluvoxamine). Enuresis is treated with imipramine, and ADHD with TCAs and atomoxetine (no mechanism taught). Nicotine dependence is treated with bupropion, and neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia with duloxetine or a TCA. GAD, social phobia, PTSD, bulimia, PMDD take an SSRI.

Points that carry questions
  • TCA overdose is the 3 C's: coma, convulsions, cardiac arrhythmias; treat with IV sodium bicarbonate, which counters the QRS widening of sodium channel block.
  • Amitriptyline is the agent to avoid after angina and a recent MI.
  • SSRI-induced sexual dysfunction: add bupropion; give the SSRI after breakfast for nausea.
  • Serotonin syndrome diagram: tryptophan, amphetamines, MAOIs, uptake blockers, 5-HT agonists.
  • Do not restrain an agitated patient: it worsens rigidity and hyperthermia.
  • Cortisol down regulates BDNF; hippocampus smaller, fewer neurons and dendritic sprouts.
  • Lithium: Ebstein anomaly in pregnancy; avoid in sick sinus syndrome and nursing mothers.
  • Hold suicide precautions until suicidal ideation is excluded.

7. Sedative-Hypnotics

Lecture scope: Lecture 7: sedation, hypnosis and the stages of sleep, the GABA-A receptor and how benzodiazepines and barbiturates enhance it, the non-GABA agents (buspirone, propranolol, ramelteon, suvorexant, modafinil), the Z drugs for insomnia, and the clinical picture, management and flumazenil reversal of benzodiazepine and barbiturate overdose, with dependence and withdrawal compared.

Slide decks: Pharm 7, Sedative and Hypnotics (37 Qs)

Sedative-hypnotics depress the CNS in a dose-dependent way. Sedation lowers alertness without inducing sleep, hypnosis resembles natural sleep but the person can be aroused by a strong stimulus, and higher doses give general anaesthesia (slides 7 and 8). Most of the drugs work on the GABA-A receptor, a five-subunit chloride channel in which GABA, the major inhibitory transmitter, binds at the alpha/beta interfaces and benzodiazepines bind at the alpha/gamma interface (slide 14). Benzodiazepines raise the receptor's affinity for GABA and increase the frequency of chloride channel opening, so chloride conduction rises and the neuron hyperpolarizes (slide 25). Barbiturates lengthen the duration of opening and, at higher doses, open the channel directly (slide 15).

Benzodiazepines are preferred to barbiturates as sedatives and hypnotics: they have a flat dose-response curve, whereas barbiturates have a steep one that runs on to coma (slides 31 and 33). The Z drugs (zolpidem, zaleplon, zopiclone, eszopiclone) are not benzodiazepines but act at the alpha 1 benzodiazepine site, disturb sleep architecture least and have the least abuse potential. Other agents act away from GABA-A: buspirone at 5-HT1A, ramelteon at melatonin receptors, suvorexant at orexin receptors, and propranolol as a beta blocker for the peripheral signs of anxiety.

High-Yield Notes

Both benzodiazepines (BZDs) and barbiturates enhance GABA-A function, but they differ in how far the CNS depression goes, what they do to sleep, and what happens in overdose. Flumazenil, a selective competitive antagonist of BZDs, is given IV to reverse BZD anaesthesia and BZD overdose; action starts in seconds and lasts 1 to 2 hours, with an elimination half life of 1 hour.

Read this table by column to see how the three classes of GABA-A enhancer differ in the points the questions turn on: where each acts, what it does to REM sleep and dependence, and whether an antidote exists. The Z drug column is the one the insomnia questions turn on, and the last row shows that flumazenil reverses benzodiazepine and Z drug overdose while barbiturate poisoning has no antidote.

FeatureBenzodiazepinesBarbituratesZ drugs
Action on GABA-ARaise GABA affinity; frequency of opening upDuration of opening up; direct chloride action at high doseAct on the alpha 1 BZD site
Dose-response and sleepFlat curve; the slide says no effect on REM sleep (they reduce it only slightly), less hangoverSteep curve to coma; marked REM suppression, rebound REM on withdrawalLeast disruption of sleep architecture
Enzymes and abuseNot enzyme inducers; the slide says low abuse liability, but tolerance and dependence occur, less than with barbituratesPotent enzyme inducers; tolerance, physical and psychological dependenceLeast abuse potential
Other actionsAnxiolytic, anticonvulsant, muscle relaxant, amnesiaAnticonvulsant, anaesthesia; amnesia with automatism, hyperalgesiaWeak anxiolytic; negligible anticonvulsant, relaxant and amnesic action
OverdoseSpecific antagonist flumazenilNo antidote; support vitals, charcoal, alkaline diuresisAntagonized by flumazenil

Benzodiazepines are used for anxiety, insomnia, preanaesthetic medication, muscle relaxation, seizures and alcohol withdrawal. Midazolam is the parenteral agent on the slide and the others are given orally (midazolam also has oral forms, so slide 26 oversimplifies); they are metabolised mainly by CYP3A4 and CYP2C19, cross the BBB and are contraindicated in pregnancy (slide 26 ties this to the BBB; the concern is crossing the placenta). Adverse effects are dose-related drowsiness and psychomotor impairment, with cardiac arrest on fast IV injection; withdrawal brings anxiety, insomnia, headache, irritability, tremors and palpitation, so doses are tapered. Flunitrazepam has an amnesic effect and is misused in sexual assault. Alcohol, hypnotics and neuroleptics add to the CNS depression, cimetidine and ketoconazole enhance BZD action, while smoking and aminophylline reduce it. Insomnia is difficulty falling asleep, more night wakefulness or short sleep: transient (under 7 days), short term (1 to 3 weeks) or long term (over 3 weeks). Sleep hygiene comes first, and hypnotics are used at the lowest dose or intermittently.

Read the Z drug table as a comparison of half life, preferred use and next day effect. Zaleplon has the shortest half life at 1 hour and zopiclone the longest of the three at 5 hours, and zolpidem and zaleplon are preferred in sleep onset insomnia.

DrugHalf life, classPreferred useNext day, adverse effects

Zaleplon1 hr (shortest); pyrazolopyrimidineSleep onset insomniaNo morning sedation, so usable when awake in the night; no tolerance, no rebound insomnia

EszopicloneActive enantiomer of zopiclone; longer actingShort and long term use, up to 1 yearNo next day effects; tolerance and dependence least; bitter taste

Read this table by drug to match each non-GABA agent to its target and its use. Buspirone and propranolol treat anxiety, melatonin and ramelteon act on melatonin receptors, and suvorexant blocks orexin receptors. Modafinil is listed with the sedative-hypnotics but promotes wakefulness rather than sleep.

Points that carry questions
  • Barbiturates: ultrashort thiopental is the induction agent (slide 19) and methohexital is the other ultrashort agent (slide 13); long-acting phenobarbital is the anticonvulsant, and enzyme induction raises glucuronyl transferase, treating neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia (less kernicterus).
  • Barbiturates are contraindicated in liver or kidney disease, severe pulmonary insufficiency and acute intermittent porphyria (induction of ALA-synthetase). They induce metabolism of warfarin, steroids, OCP and tolbutamide, and phenobarbitone reduces griseofulvin absorption.
  • Acute barbiturate poisoning is flabby coma with shallow respiration and low BP; sodium bicarbonate alkaline diuresis, haemodialysis and hemoperfusion are used.
  • Plasma protein binding differs: flurazepam 10%, diazepam 99%. Chlordiazepoxide was the first BZD (Sternbach, 1955).
  • Stage 4 sleep (10 to 20%): growth hormone is high and night terrors occur.
  • Epilepsy and Huntington's disease involve a lack of inhibitory GABA.

8. Alcohol and Substance Abuse

Lecture scope: Small group discussion cases on substance misuse and alcohol: precipitated opioid withdrawal, cocaine and dissociative drug mechanisms, benzodiazepine reversal seizures, alcohol withdrawal in cirrhosis, disulfiram-like reactions, methanol poisoning, acetaminophen toxicity in heavy drinkers, Wernicke encephalopathy and relapse prevention.

Slide decks: Pharm SGD, Substance Abuse and Alcohols (15 Qs)

Substance misuse and alcohol are examined here through the school's small group case sheet, so the section is built from its ten cases rather than from a lecture deck. Each case turns on one recognition step: an opioid that precipitates withdrawal, a drug that blocks monoamine reuptake, a dissociative agent, a benzodiazepine reversal that provokes seizures, or one of the alcohol problems of withdrawal, metabolism, poisoning and relapse prevention.

Alcohol is oxidised by alcohol dehydrogenase to acetaldehyde, which aldehyde dehydrogenase clears. Anything that blocks the second step, such as disulfiram or an antimicrobial given for trichomoniasis, lets acetaldehyde accumulate and causes flushing, throbbing headache, nausea, palpitations and low blood pressure. Chronic drinking also induces CYP2E1, which is why ordinary doses of acetaminophen can injure the liver of a heavy drinker.

High-Yield Notes

The case sheet gives no key, so the answers below are the standard teaching for each scenario. Buprenorphine is a partial mu agonist: given to a patient dependent on a full agonist such as methadone, it precipitates withdrawal (rhinorrhea, yawning, piloerection, cramps, diarrhea, dilated pupils), whereas morphine, oxycodone and hydromorphone would only add to the effect. A white powder that numbs the gums with a hyperadrenergic picture is cocaine, which blocks reuptake of norepinephrine, dopamine and serotonin. Agitation with nystagmus, no response to pain and amnesia points to a noncompetitive NMDA antagonist (phencyclidine type).

A patient dependent on alprazolam who is given an intravenous reversal agent breathes better, then seizes: the competitive GABA-A (benzodiazepine site) antagonist flumazenil removes the drug abruptly and precipitates withdrawal. Alcohol withdrawal with confusion, fever, tremor and hallucinations at 72 hours is treated with a benzodiazepine, and with cirrhosis the one chosen is lorazepam, because diazepam and chlordiazepoxide rely on hepatic oxidation to long-acting active metabolites and accumulate.

Read the table row by row to separate the alcohol-related poisonings and interactions by the compound that accumulates and the clue that identifies it, then read across to the key feature used to answer the question. Each row names a different agent and mechanism, so match the clinical clue first.

SituationCulpritIdentifying clue
Wine after an antimicrobial for trichomoniasisAcetaldehyde accumulation (aldehyde dehydrogenase blocked)Flushing, throbbing headache, nausea, palpitations, low BP within 30 minutes
Unlabeled garage liquidFormic acid from methanolBlurred vision, optic disc hyperemia, high anion gap acidosis, raised osmolal gap, no urine crystals
Daily drinker on therapeutic acetaminophenCYP2E1 induction raises the toxic metaboliteJaundice, right upper quadrant pain, AST and ALT in the thousands

Three drugs are named for alcohol use disorder, and the clinical setting chooses between them. Read the Role column first, then the Choose-when column, which carries the exam discriminator for each case.

DrugRoleChoose when
AcamprosateRelapse prevention after detoxificationRenal function is normal; it is the choice when the patient takes an opioid daily
NaltrexoneRelapse prevention, opioid receptor antagonistAvoid in a patient on daily oxycodone, because it precipitates opioid withdrawal

Points that carry questions
  • Confusion, lateral rectus weakness and a wide-based gait in a malnourished drinker (foul-smelling breath) is Wernicke encephalopathy: give thiamine before or with glucose (SGD, question 9), not folic acid, cyanocobalamin or a benzodiazepine.
  • Tramadol, oxycodone, hydromorphone and morphine are the other analgesics in the case; none is the partial agonist that precipitates withdrawal in a methadone patient.
  • Propranolol and buspirone appear as distractors only; neither prevents withdrawal seizures or delirium.
